Please remember the early registration deadline for the Tampa
introductory distance sampling workshop is 1 September.  Please complete
your registration by that date so we know how many participants we will
have (and so we can pay the venue deposit for the Marriott Tampa

while attending the workshop.

messages.subject: Survey effort clarification
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

One point that I still find confusing is what values ultimately go into
the survey effort column.  I have 45 point count circles spread across
three habitat types (15 in each habitat class).  Each point was always
surveyed 6 times a year for two years.

Is effort always going to be 6 regardless of how many visits I actually
recorded the target species?  For instance, some points counts had a bird
or birds on 2 of the 6 visits.  Is effort then 2 for that point count or
do I keep it as 6 and enter blank fields for the other 4 visit
observations  What happens if a bird species is only ever seen on 15 of
the 45 points counts?  Do I still keep all 45 point counts in the data
file with blanks under each visit and observation layer?

>From other forum responses it seems like effort should always be the total
# of visits to a site with blanks created for visits without a sighting.
I would appreciate knowing for sure which is right.

Thank you!

--
Julian D. Avery
Rutgers University

--

messages.subject: Re: Survey effort clarification
messages.body_plain:
Julian:

Effort, for point counts, is indeed measured as the effort you expended
trying to detect birds (whether you detected them or not).  So if you
made 6 visits but were only successful on 2 visits you indeed record 6
as the amount of effort you expended.

You would get a very inflated (and very wrong) estimate of bird density
if you entered your effort as only the number of visits during which you
detected animals.  A visit without a detection is still effort expended
by you attempting to detect birds.

The same applies for line transect situations; if you walked 25 1km
transects hoping to detect animals, and only detected them on 5
transects, you would not record the total amount of effort expended as
5km, but rather 25km.

The answer to your final question is yes: keep all 45 points in the data
file even though there were detections made at 15 of them; leave the
other 30 blank.

messages.subject: Re: visual estimation of distance
messages.body_plain:
Sharon,

I would suggest that you examine the histogram of distances by using
various bin interval sizes (preferably smaller bin intervals). Then
inspect these histograms for evidence of "heaping" caused by what is
termed 'digit preference' where observers prefer to classify distances
at intervals like 10, 15, 20, 25, etc. If you find evidence of digit
preference then select your bin intervals so that they encompass values
where heaping occurs. Increasing the size of bins at greater distances
may also help.

Look in the index to Introduction to Distance Sampling book under
'heaping' for more insight and suggestions.

Duane

On 8/24/2011 5:16 PM, Sharon wrote:
> > Hello list,
> >
> > I am working with data from a study that has already been completed. The study involved point-transect sampling of multiple species of birds. Distances were estimated by eye as exact distances (not categorized into intervals). Buckland et al (2001) indicates that visual estimation alone should be avoided but recognizes that in some cases it may be necessary.  Prior to data collection in each year, observers were trained on estimating distances to objects in the field by practicing estimating distances to objects in the field at a known distances from various points. THere are no "test" data for use in evaluating potential bias or the size of the distance estimation error.
> >
> > I am wondering how best to move forward with these data in the distance sampling framework. That is, can the observations be analyzed as exact distances without concern over potential limitations from visual estimation? If not, what are thoughts on binning the data into intervals, with larger intervals farther from the point, as well as truncating data beyond some distance at which visual estimates would be considered most unreliable?
> >
> > The study occurred over multiple years with transects sampled typically five times each spring, with different observers each sampling within a year. Across years some of the observers were the same, others were unique.

messages.subject: Post-stratification using a time x space parameter
messages.subject_clean: Post-stratification using a time x space parameter
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've got a question about post-stratification that I would value some=20
input on. We are (still :) working with a bird dataset that consists of=20
detections from three annual repeat visits to 30 locations. We have been=20
generating location-specific density estimates for each year by fitting=20
models to detections pooled over all locations, then post-stratifying by=20
location. Yet these annual datasets are not very large, and we would=20
like to take advantage of pooled data from all three years for model=20
fitting, while still deriving estimates for individual years. So a=20
stratification by year AND location would be desirable.
I thought that could be achieved by adding a year x location variable=20
(90 values) to the all-year pooled dataset and then post-stratifying by=20
this factor. However, not having used this approach before, I'm=20
uncertain whether such a combination of spatial and temporal replication=20
is asking for trouble. Specifically, it seems as if the recombination of=20
the estimates for a global density estimate would be problematic, and=20
couldn't easily be done within Distance. Would that be correct?

best regards

florian

  --
Dr Florian Weller
Centre for the Study of Agriculture, Food and Environment (CSAFE)
K=E2 Rakahau o te Ao T=FBroa
University of Otago
